title: LoRa mesh network for a whole town
summary: Turn a handful of homemade LoRa nodes into a network that carries text messages across a whole town with no phone network, internet or grid. Put a few solar-powered relays on the highest places you can reach, set roles, presets and channels so the air does not clog, protect masts from lightning and cold, and keep it running with remote checks.

materials.item: Relay nodes from the node guide, nRF52 boards (RAK WisBlock, Pro Micro DIY) preferred for solar, plus one spare
Outdoor vertical antennas for your band: ground planes from the node guide or bought ones
Low-loss 50 Ω coax (LMR-400 type) with weatherproof connectors, only where the node can't sit at the top

Batteries: protected 18650 Li-ion cells for a WisBlock base board (its charger is made for 3.7 V Li-ion cells and charges them to 4.2 V; never put a LiFePO4 cell on it); a 12 V LiFePO4 battery, or a lead-acid battery in its own vented space, for a hill site
materials.qty: 2–4 cells (4 for ten sunless days), or 1 battery

materials.item: Solar panel: 6–10 W ‘5 V’ for a WisBlock base board, with an open-circuit voltage under 5.5 V: many read 6 V or more unloaded (RAK’s own: 6.1 V ±10 %), so measure in full sun (RAK19007, RAK solar panel); or 20–100 W for a 12 V site
Charge controller with a LiFePO4 setting and a low-temperature charge cut-off (12 V sites)
12 V to 5 V USB adapter (car charger) to run a node from a 12 V battery
Fuse for every battery positive lead
Weatherproof plastic boxes with cable glands and membrane vents
Foam to wrap batteries inside the box
Mast: steel or aluminium tube, with guy ropes and U-bolts or hose clamps

Ground rod and listed clamp, and copper wire from mast to rod: 6 AWG (13.3 mm²; 16 mm² in metric cable) or heavier, flat copper strap better (10 AWG is only the code minimum); 6 AWG (13.3 mm², or 16 mm²) or heavier to bond rods together
materials.qty: 1 rod per site (more is better), wire as needed

materials.item: Listed coax surge arrester (antenna discharge unit) for every coax entering a building
INA219 or INA260 current sensor for solar telemetry

steps.text: Find out what your area already runs: scan with Local Mesh Discovery in the Meshtastic app and ask local groups. Match their region, preset and channels, or agree new ones, before anyone builds.

While the internet works, run the Meshtastic Site Planner for every candidate site and save the maps. Mark the high points on a printed town map: water towers, grain elevators, steeples, tall roofs, hills.

Visit each candidate with a handheld node and binoculars. Check that each site can see the next, and that the middle of each link has its Fresnel clearance (table in the notes). Ask the owner for permission and write down who may visit, when, and who looks after the node. Ask the owner to switch off or turn down any cell, FM, paging or microwave antennas before you go near them (TDI towers).
steps.warn: Stay off towers, water towers and roofs unless the owner agrees and a trained climber does the work, tied on, with a second person and a rescue plan: a 2 m fall can kill. Antennas on towers and roofs can give a dangerous radio dose close up (TDI towers).

steps.text: Agree the town settings and write them down: region, preset (Long Fast to start), the default primary channel kept, private secondary channels with random keys, hop limit 3. Make a QR code for the channel set and hand it out in person.

Build each relay with the node guide. On the bench set role ROUTER (ROUTER_LATE only for a cluster behind a hill, see the notes), add up to three admin keys, turn on device and power telemetry (both off by default; set each interval), then run it 2 to 6 hours on a meter that totals watt-hours to measure its draw.
steps.warn: Keep the antenna on whenever the relay is powered, on the bench too: transmitting without one can damage the radio.

steps.text: Size the battery and panel from the measured draw (worked example in the notes), for your worst winter month: about ten sunless days of battery for a relay the town relies on (FSEC batteries), and the panel facing south, tilted to about latitude + 15° (NRCan PV maps). Wire panel, charger and battery, with a fuse in the battery positive lead and a low-temperature charge cut-off.
steps.warn: Lithium cells must not be charged below 0 °C (Victron says +5 °C for LiFePO4) or above 45 °C. Shorted battery leads burn: fuse them.

steps.text: Box it: plastic box, membrane vent, cable glands, antenna outside, drip loops on every cable. Wrap the battery in foam. Seal coax connectors with tape and sealant.
steps.warn: Keep the battery in the shade of the box and the panel: lithium cells must not be charged above 45 °C, and a box in summer sun gets hot. Never seal a lead-acid battery into the box: it gives off explosive hydrogen.

steps.text: Put the antenna as high as you safely can. Mount the node at the top with a short pigtail, or use low-loss coax as short as possible. Guy the mast against wind. Work in pairs on ladders and roofs. The 0.6 m (2 ft) in electrical codes is only for a fixed lead-in from circuits of 250 V or less (3 m, 10 ft, above that), not a safe distance for raising a mast (Mike Holt NEC 810).
steps.warn: Keep the mast and antenna at least twice their combined height from every overhead power line, and treat every line as live: a mast that touches one can kill everyone touching it or standing near (RSGB antenna safety). Can’t keep that distance? Pick another site.

steps.text: Ground the mast to a ground rod with copper wire run as straight as possible; put a listed coax arrester where any coax enters a building; bond an extra rod to the building's ground (details in the notes).
steps.warn: Never climb, touch or work on a mast, its coax or its ground wire when thunder can be heard, nor until 30 minutes after the last (NOAA lightning). Disconnect the coax before a storm, never during one (ARRL Field Day).

steps.text: Range test every hop: set a router to send every 30 s (Long Fast) or 15 s (Medium), then walk or drive each district with a receiving node and note where messages stop. Run a traceroute from the far side of town and note each hop's SNR. Fill gaps with a CLIENT_BASE node on a roof (mark the nodes it serves as favourites), or a ROUTER_LATE only for a cluster behind a hill, then turn the range test off (Meshtastic range test).

Teach the town: everyone else stays CLIENT, second radios in a house go CLIENT_MUTE, and home bases with a roof antenna go CLIENT_BASE, with the nodes they serve marked as favourites (it acts as a CLIENT for everyone else). Nobody else sets ROUTER or raises the hop limit.

Check telemetry weekly: falling battery voltage means snow, shade or a failing battery. Telemetry is off until you turn it on, and a router sends it no more often than every 12 h, so ask a relay for a fresh reading when you need one (Meshtastic DeviceTelemetry.cpp). Visit each site before freeze-up and after storms. When channel use (ChUtil) often passes 25 %, where the firmware starts holding back its own broadcasts, or the mesh passes about 60 close nodes, lengthen broadcast intervals first (see the operations guide), then plan a preset change for every node at once.
steps.warn: Check batteries at each visit: a swollen, leaking or hot lithium cell is finished and can catch fire.

notes:
Build each node with [Build a LoRa mesh node from parts](#guides/build_lora_node). Frequency and power rules: [LoRa bands](#ref/reference_lora_bands); antenna gain counts against the legal limit, so a high-gain antenna on a mast can mean turning the radio down.

## Height beats power

Terrain is the biggest limit on range, and the best way to get more is to raise the antenna (Site planner blog). Meshtastic's role advice prefers a tower on a peak to a tall building (Meshtastic role blog). Line-of-sight distance from height is worked out in the [Yagi guide](#guides/build_yagi_antenna).

**Radio horizon.** The rule there, d (km) ≈ 4.1 × (√h1 + √h2) with heights in metres, is plain geometry on an Earth given 4/3 of its real 6,370 km radius, which allows for the air bending radio waves down (ITU-R P.834): √(2 × 4/3 × 6,370 km × h m ÷ 1,000) = 4.12 √h. With no bending it is 3.57 √h. For LoRa heights, with 4.12, calculated for this guide:

| Link | Horizon |
|---|---|
| Handheld at 1.5 m (5 ft) to handheld | 10 km (6 mi) |
| Handheld to a 10 m (33 ft) roof | 18 km (11 mi) |
| Handheld to a 30 m (100 ft) mast | 28 km (17 mi) |
| Mast to mast, both 30 m | 45 km (28 mi) |

That is a ceiling over smooth ground, not a promise: hills, buildings and the Fresnel zone below cut it down. A 30 m mast is tower work for trained climbers: see the climbing warning in the steps.

**The Fresnel zone, in plain words.** The signal doesn't travel down a thin line. It fills a cigar-shaped space between the two antennas, fattest in the middle. Trees, roofs or ground poking into it weaken the link even when you can see the far mast. Keep at least 60 % of its radius clear (RF Cafe). Radius in the middle (m) = 8.66 × √(link km ÷ GHz), calculated for this guide:

| Link | 915 MHz radius | Keep clear (60 %) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 km | 9 m (30 ft) | 5 m (18 ft) |
| 2 km | 13 m (42 ft) | 8 m (25 ft) |
| 5 km | 20 m (66 ft) | 12 m (40 ft) |
| 10 km | 29 m (94 ft) | 17 m (56 ft) |

At 868 MHz it is about 3 % more (√(915 ÷ 868) = 1.027); at 433 MHz multiply by 1.45.

The Meshtastic Site Planner maps coverage from terrain data, about 90 m resolution, with no buildings or trees: enter an average clutter height (10 m for towns) and check its maps by real tests (Meshtastic site planner, Site planner blog). It streams its terrain data, so run it for every candidate site while the internet works and save the maps.

## How far it really reaches

**Link budget** adds up everything between two radios: transmit power + both antenna gains − cable and connector losses − the receiver's sensitivity. What is left after the path losses is the **fade margin**, kept in hand for fading from reflections, movement and weather (Semtech AN1200.22, Campbell link budget, Site planner blog). Long Fast's 153 dB assumes 22 dBm and 0 dBi antennas (Meshtastic presets); the receiver hears down to about −130 dBm (Meshtastic site planner). For a link that must not fail, aim for a fade margin of 20–30 dB; under 10 dB, raise the antennas or fit better ones (Campbell link budget). Work out your own links on the [LoRa calculator](#ref/lora_airtime).

**Free space is wildly optimistic.** Free-space loss (dB) = 32.4 + 20 log f (MHz) + 20 log d (km) (ITU-R P.525), so Long Fast's 153 dB would carry about 1,200 km (730 mi) at 915 MHz, calculated for this guide. "Free space" means no ground and no obstacles at all; near the ground, past a critical distance, loss grows with the fourth power of distance instead of the square (Campbell link budget). Every 6 dB lost halves free-space range (20 log 2 = 6, calculated for this guide).

**What the town takes.** Median extra loss at 915 MHz, calculated for this guide from the ITU model named:

| What | Extra loss |
|---|---|
| Handheld at 1.5 m (5 ft) among houses (10 m, 33 ft, clutter) | 19 dB at that end (ITU-R P.2108) |
| Handheld among 15 m (50 ft) buildings or trees | 23 dB at that end (ITU-R P.2108) |
| Antenna above the roofs and trees | None at that end (ITU-R P.2108) |
| Indoors, traditional building | 14 dB (ITU-R P.2109) |
| Indoors, thermally efficient building (metallised glass, foil-backed panels) | 31 dB (ITU-R P.2109) |
| One end 50 m (160 ft) into woodland | 7 dB (ITU-R P.833) |
| One end 200 m (660 ft) into woodland | 19 dB (ITU-R P.833) |
| Hilltop just touching the line between the antennas | 6 dB (ITU-R P.526) |
| Hilltop one Fresnel radius (table above) over that line | 16 dB, more if rounded (ITU-R P.526) |

The woodland figures come from mixed forest at 949 MHz. Loss through trees changes with species, density, water content and wind, and trees in leaf cost about 20 % more per metre than bare ones (ITU-R P.833), so test links in summer. Two handhelds on the street pay clutter loss at both ends; a router above the clutter pays none at its end, which is why height wins.

**Examples, not promises.** The Intermountain Mesh expects 1.6–8 km (1–5 mi) in typical terrain from client nodes at ground level or on house roofs, not routers; the page gives their height as 8–11 m (25–35 ft) in one place and up to 30 m (100 ft) in another (Freq51 routers). In Shinjuku, Tokyo, a +13 dBm LoRa link (SF8) still got 9 packets in 10 through at 1.35 km (0.8 mi) and none at 1.75 km (1.1 mi) (Semtech AN1200.22). Wellington's longest permanent link, between two high sites, is 254 km (158 mi) (Meshtastic LongFast blog); the ground record is 331 km (206 mi), set on the slower Very Long Slow preset at 868 MHz, not Long Fast (Meshtastic range tests).

## Roles: few routers

| Role (Meshtastic roles) | Use |
|---|---|
| CLIENT | The default. Relays only when no other node has |
| CLIENT_MUTE | Extra radios in one house, crowded spots. Never relays |
| CLIENT_BASE | Home base with a roof antenna. Always relays for its favourite nodes |
| ROUTER | Fixed relays on the best sites. Always rebroadcasts once |
| ROUTER_LATE | For a cluster of nodes behind a hill or in a canyon, or a site that must relay but covers little of the wider mesh. Not for a rooftop or the inside of a house (use CLIENT_BASE), and not for a busy Long Fast mesh. Always rebroadcasts once, after the other roles have had their chance. Watch channel use (ChUtil) under 25 % and transmit airtime (AirUtilTX) under 7–8 % (Meshtastic ROUTER_LATE blog) |
| REPEATER | Deprecated from firmware 2.7.11: use ROUTER |

Routers are only for stationary nodes in very strategic places. Too many neighbouring routers transmit at once and collide; a badly placed one uses up hops before a packet reaches a better site, so some groups can send but get no replies. Raising the hop limit to cover that only adds airtime (Meshtastic role blog). The default hop limit is 3, the maximum 7, and "3 is fine" (Meshtastic LoRa). An ESP32 router turns power saving on, which switches Bluetooth off (Meshtastic roles, Meshtastic power): set it up over USB.

**How many, and where.** One very high site may cover a small town. A bigger one needs several routers on the highest points, spread apart; the right number comes from your range tests, not a rule (the Meshtastic role blog gives none). The Bay Area mesh reserves router mode for high-elevation nodes and sometimes puts two at opposite ends of an area (Meshtastic LongFast blog). Every street should see a router and each router should hear the next. Client, router, router, client uses 2 of the 3 hops. On firmware 2.7.11 or later, routers that list each other as favourites do not spend a hop on the link between them (Meshtastic zero-cost hops). Ask site owners while there is someone to ask.

**Overlap, but not too much.** Don't build a chain: in a tree-shaped network a node that drops out cuts off every branch behind it, while a mesh has several routes (AREDN topology). Give each router a path to two others where you can, and let the districts that matter most hear two routers (the Bay Area's pairs at opposite ends of an area are meant for a better chance of line of sight, as above). Stop there: the Bay Area uses its high routers to cover widely without needless redundancy (Meshtastic LongFast blog), and too many neighbouring routers collide (above). If two routers' Site Planner maps cover nearly the same streets, make one a CLIENT. One big-city group, the Twin Cities mesh, accepts a router only with its antenna at least 27.4 m (90 ft) up, a full 360° view and direct two-way links to at least 5 other ROUTER or ROUTER_LATE nodes, and asks its members to review the site first (MSP Mesh roles). That is a big-city rule: a small town's few routers will not meet it. Airtime and congestion: [running the mesh](#guides/skill_lora_mesh_operations).

## Presets and airtime

| Preset | Data rate | Link budget |
|---|---|---|
| Long Fast (default) | 1.07 kbps | 153 dB |
| Medium Slow | 1.95 kbps | 150.5 dB |
| Medium Fast | 3.52 kbps | 148 dB |
| Short Fast | 10.94 kbps | 143 dB |

Figures at 22 dBm and 0 dBi. Each step up in spreading factor doubles airtime; 500 kHz Turbo presets are not legal everywhere (Meshtastic presets). Consider leaving Long Fast past about 60 nodes close together or heavy traffic: Wellington's busy sites passed 65 % channel use; the Bay Area's 150-plus nodes run Medium Slow (Meshtastic LongFast blog). Every node must change together: nodes on different presets have no link at any distance (Meshtastic joining).

## Channels and keys

- Keep the default primary channel. Its key is public, so anyone can read it (Meshtastic channels), but strangers and newcomers can find you, and renaming the primary changes the frequency (Meshtastic joining).
- Put town traffic on secondary channels (up to 7) with random 256-bit keys, such as "town" and "medics" (Meshtastic channels). Hand out the QR codes face to face.
- Public channels share position at 15 bits at most; 13 bits is about 2.9 km, 19 bits about 45 m (Meshtastic channels).
- Routers relay other meshes on the same settings by default (ALL), even encrypted traffic. LOCAL_ONLY stops a router relaying channels it does not carry (the public primary channel it does carry is still relayed); KNOWN_ONLY also ignores nodes missing from its node list (Meshtastic roles).

**Remote admin.** From firmware 2.5, store your admin node's public key in each relay's Security settings, up to three keys (the Web client takes only one; use the Android or Apple app or the command line). The old channel named "admin" only manages pre-2.5 nodes. Try changes on a bench node first: a bad setting can cut a relay off (Meshtastic remote admin).

## Power for relay sites

A relay listens all day, so receive current sets the budget: the RAK4631 draws 17 mA receiving and 92 mA sending at 17 dBm; its datasheet prints the 20 dBm transmit figure garbled, and a node left at the default transmit power sends at the module's 22 dBm maximum, where the RAK19007 base board lists 130 mA (RAK4631, RAK19007). Its 2.0 µA sleep helps only nodes that sleep. Meshtastic says nRF52 boards draw less than ESP32 (Meshtastic devices); a Heltec V3 (ESP32) router still averaged 0.046 W at 5 % airtime (Kaspars solar). Measure yours for 2 to 6 hours with a meter that totals watt-hours (Meshtastic measure power).

**Worked example** ([Power budget](#ref/reference_power_budget) method): 17 mA × 3.7 V × 24 h = 1.5 Wh a day, plus 25 % = 1.9 Wh (that margin covers transmitting about 4 % of the day at 130 mA; a busy router needs your own measurement instead). Five sunless days, half capacity in deep cold, 80 % usable: 1.9 × 5 × 2 ÷ 0.8 ≈ 24 Wh, two 12 Wh 18650s (Samsung 35E). Five days is near the top of the usual range: autonomy, the days a full battery runs the load with no sun, is typically 2–6 days for ordinary systems, and can be over ten for an essential load, public safety or where the weather demands it, and a bigger battery is cycled less deeply (FSEC batteries). For a relay the town relies on, plan ten: 1.9 × 10 × 2 ÷ 0.8 ≈ 48 Wh, four 18650s. Panel: 1.9 ÷ (1 winter sun hour × 0.75) ≈ 2.5 W. One hour is well above what Whitehorse gets in December (0.70, or 0.74 tilted to latitude + 15°), which needs 1.9 ÷ (0.70 × 0.75) ≈ 3.6 W; the southern cities in the table below get 1.6 to 2.9. Kaspars' 4 W panel gave under 1 W in winter (Kaspars solar): fit 6–10 W. The RAK19007's solar input takes 4.4–5.5 V and charges at up to 350 mA (Meshtastic RAK base; RAK's own datasheet gives 350 mA only for USB charging and no solar figure), about 1.3 Wh per hour of full sun at 3.7 V. The panel's open-circuit voltage must stay under 5.5 V or the board can be damaged (RAK19007), and a '5 V' panel often reads higher unloaded. Marginal in a northern winter. For a site that must not fail, run the node from a [12 V solar system](#guides/build_solar_12v_system) through a 12-to-5 V USB adapter, with no Li-ion cell fitted to the node board (the board would charge it from the adapter, cold or not), and measure the whole thing.

**Winter sun in Canada.** NRCan's maps give the mean daily sun on a south-facing panel for each month, from 1974–1993 records, in kWh/m² a day (NRCan PV maps); 1 kWh/m² ÷ 1 kW/m² of full sun = 1 hour. December:

| Place | Tilt = latitude | Latitude + 15° | Flat (0°) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vancouver | 1.61 | 1.71 | 0.68 |
| Calgary | 2.85 | 3.07 | 0.90 |
| Toronto | 2.21 | 2.35 | 1.19 |
| Halifax | 2.27 | 2.43 | 1.09 |
| Whitehorse | 0.70 | 0.74 | 0.19 |

These are long-term averages; a dark spell is what the battery days are for (FSEC batteries). NRCan's own output figures come to the same 0.75 of these hours (Calgary: 66 kWh/kWp ÷ 31 days ÷ 2.85, calculated for this guide). For other places use the [solar calculator](#ref/solar).

**Tilt and snow.** Face the panel south and tilt it steeply: in December latitude + 15° beats latitude tilt everywhere in the table, and a flat panel gets about half or less (NRCan PV maps). Steep panels should shed snow sooner; Sandia's snow poster says so only in passing, about the high tilt of its trackers (Sandia snow). In a five-year Edmonton test, snow cost about 3 % of the energy, far below the 20 % once assumed; the article does not say how that splits between summer and winter. Fixed panels at 14°, 18°, 27°, 45°, 53° and 90° were compared: 45° did best with snow, 53° (about the latitude) was most efficient, and the vertical one was worst, 24 % down. Latitude + 15° was not tested, so it is a winter choice (NAIT snow). Clear snow only where you can do it safely from the ground; never climb a roof or mast for it. NAIT's team advises against clearing panels on pitched roofs (NAIT snow).

## Cold batteries

- Li-ion and LiFePO4 charge only from 0 to 45 °C (Samsung 35E, PSL LiFePO4). Victron allows LiFePO4 charging only from +5 °C and wants chargers switched off below that, ideally by the battery's BMS (Victron LiFePO4).
- Discharge: Li-ion down to −10 °C (Samsung 35E), LiFePO4 to −20 °C (PSL LiFePO4), though Victron says rated capacity drops about 20 % at 0 °C and to about 50 % at −20 °C (Victron LiFePO4). A LiFePO4 18650 holds only about 4.8 Wh (PSL's 1.5 Ah cell), against 12 Wh for a Li-ion 18650, so the worked example needs about 2.5 times the cells.
- The RAK19007 has no battery temperature sensing that its datasheet mentions (RAK19007), so a Li-ion cell on it will charge in freezing weather. Foam only slows the cooling. If the box can fall below 0 °C, use the 12 V LiFePO4 system with a charge controller or BMS that stops charging in the cold (Victron uses a BMS on/off port), or a Li-ion pack whose protection board has a low-temperature charge cut-off, and size for half capacity. See [Battery chemistries](#ref/reference_battery_chemistry).

## Boxes

Plastic, with the antenna outside: metal cases cut range badly (Ebyte E22). Sealed boxes pull in damp air as they heat and cool; a membrane vent stops that (Hylec vents). A lead-acid battery, even a sealed one, can give off hydrogen, which explodes at about 4 % in air: never seal one inside a box, and give it open ventilation (DesignSpark lead-acid). Coax entries through glands, with drip loops.

**Near the antenna.** A node at 22 dBm is a small radio hazard, but keep people at least 1 m (3 ft) from an antenna that is transmitting. The US general-public limit at 915 MHz is 0.61 mW/cm² (FCC 1.1310); an antenna at the legal 4 W EIRP reaches it at about 0.23 m, calculated for this guide in free space, and rooftops reflect. The bigger radio hazard on a shared tower or roof is other operators' transmitters, not yours (see the climbing warning).

## Lightning and grounding

US rules, NEC Article 810, with section numbers from the 2017 edition as summarised by Mike Holt (Mike Holt NEC 810); later editions may number them differently, and the inspector decides:

- Ground masts and metal supports (810.15). Never fix an antenna to the power service mast (810.12).
- Antennas and lead-ins at least 0.6 m (2 ft) from exposed power wires (810.13); lead-ins must not be able to swing closer than 0.6 m (2 ft) to circuits of 250 V or less, or 3 m (10 ft) to higher-voltage ones, and 1.8 m (6 ft) from a lightning protection system (810.18(A)). These are minimums for a fixed installation, not a safe distance for raising a mast.
- A listed antenna discharge unit (coax arrester) on every lead-in, nearest where it enters the building (810.20, 810.57).
- Bonding wire: copper, no smaller than 10 AWG ([5.3 mm²](#ref/reference_wire_gauge)) by code (810.21(H)); for lightning use 6 AWG ([13.3 mm²](#ref/reference_wire_gauge)) or heavier, flat copper strap if you can (SCC ARES lightning). Run it as straight as possible with as few bends as possible, because lightning won't take corners, and protect it from damage (810.21(D), (E)).
- An extra ground rod for the antenna is bonded to the building's ground with at least 6 AWG (13.3 mm²) (810.21(J)).

Bring every arrester and ground to one single point at the entry, don't operate with lightning nearby (SCC ARES lightning), and disconnect antennas from equipment at the first sign of a storm (ARRL Field Day). Canada's Electrical Code has its own rules, so don't carry the US section numbers over; ask the owner's electrician or inspector. At a site with no building, take mast and arrester straight to a ground rod, and add more rods about two rod-lengths apart, bonded together, if you can: ARRL's advice is a network of rods, not one (ARRL lightning part 3).

## Keeping it running

- Device telemetry sends battery level, voltage, channel use and airtime. It is off by default in firmware 2.7.26, and a clean node's interval is "never": turn it on and set the interval too (changing the role to ROUTER sets 12 h). On the default channel a router sends it no more often than every 12 h and a client every 30 minutes (Meshtastic NodeDB.cpp). An INA219 or INA260 adds solar current (Meshtastic telemetry). Ask a relay for a fresh reading with `meshtastic --request-telemetry --dest '!nodeid'`. Log it weekly.
- Traceroute shows each hop's SNR; one per 30 s per sender, and costly in airtime (Meshtastic traceroute).
- Visit sites before freeze-up and after storms.
- Running it: [Run and grow a town LoRa mesh](#guides/skill_lora_mesh_operations). Handing over: [Hand over a town LoRa mesh](#guides/skill_lora_mesh_handover).

## MeshCore

Another firmware, with fixed repeaters: only repeaters relay, companion radios never (a room server can too, with `set repeat on`, but the FAQ discourages it). A first message floods, later ones follow the remembered route, up to 64 hops; channel (group) messages always flood. US and Canada preset: 910.525 MHz, SF7, 62.5 kHz, coding rate 5, as the FAQ stood in October 2025; regions revise their presets, so take the one in your region's app. Repeaters ship with the admin password "password": change it (MeshCore FAQ, MeshCore README). A radio runs one firmware or the other.

## This guide on the mesh

A computer running this guide's hub beside a Meshtastic node answers ?guide and ?step questions over the air and passes field notes between camps (docs/LORA.md; not yet tried on a real radio).
